newsitem.title: UK: Cobalt fails to stir on Gecamines comments.
newsitem.headline: Cobalt fails to stir on Gecamines comments.

text.p: News that Congo's state mining company Gecamines has a two-month stockpile of around 670 tonnes of cobalt and was trying to sell it failed to make any serious dent in a European market that was entering the traditionally slow summer period.
Gecamines chairman Mbaka Kawaya said in an interview from Mauritius that the company would air freight cobalt which had already been sold.

One London based trader said that the delivery of material into Europe could add to pressure on prices that have recently been easing against the backdrop of pricing operations and a slowing in consumer demand.
"There are enough units on the ground in Europe to meet demand ...there may be some easing in the price but I believe it is close to bottoming out," this trader said.
One source with close contacts in the Democratic Republic of the Congo expressed doubt on the figure of 670 tonnes as he believed that it was a projection of 1996 figures.
According to this source the amount of material Gecamines holds now is around 200 tonnes of off grade material.
"Production has been much lower over the last six months...I believe Gecamines are trying to tell consumers that they are still in business and able to move material," the source said.
Another trading source said even if 670 tonnes of material is moved it could not satisfy demand for agreed long-term contracts, most of which centre on Japan.
The trading source said that Gecamines available stock in Europe was extremely low and not of high grade standard.
"Instead of Gecamines trying to bolster consumer confidence they should be sorting out their transport problems," a European trader said.
Congo continues to experience problems with rail transport through Zambia to South Africa which is used to export cobalt and copper.
Zambia stopped cross-border railway traffic because of a dispute over debts and effectively froze exports from the mineral-rich region of Shaba.
"Gecamines can not move metal by rail so that is why they are using airfreight," a trader said.

Gecamines also said they expected copper and cobalt output to drop in 1997 from last year's production levels. But Gecamines chairman Mbaka Kawaya told Reuters he expected output to increase next year.
"We will not realise this year the same production as last year but we will increase production (next year). The increase in production will probably start the second half of the year," Kawaya said .
High grade cobalt is assessed now around $23/$24 a pound, while lower grade Russian material stood near $19/$20
